# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-7 (Extended v80)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 2, approximately late 1825 or late 1826)**: Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary at Convent of Petit-Picpus. Earlier markers: 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, Valjean's theft and flight; Waterloo/Hougomont June 17-18); 1817 (young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral tenure); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest; Javert's revelation; TRIAL SEQUENCE in Arras; Valjean's self-revelation; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. before six a.m.; Fantine's death; Valjean arrested beside death-bed; VALJEAN ESCAPES same evening)**; December 1823 (Montfermeil rescue of Cosette, 1,500-franc payment to Thénardier); **December 26, 1823 (Valjean and Cosette returned to Paris via Barrier Monceaux)**; 1824 spring onward (decrepit building lodging; winter passed; spring advanced); **Summer Year 2**: Achieved sanctuary inside walled garden compound, le Petit-Picpus district.

## Primary Locations
M. sur M.; Montfermeil (between Livry and Chelles); English harbor towns (Dunstead/Kelford/Ravenmere/Staveford); Arras; Waterloo; Toulon; Paris districts including Mouffetard quarter (Rue Censier, Rue Copeau, Rue du Battoir-Saint-Victor, Rue du Puits l'Ermite, Rue de Pontoise; commissary office No. 14; Saint-Étienne-du-Mont church); **Gorbeau House** (Rue de la Cosette area, Mouffetard): Decrepit lodging, old woman portress, Javert's surveillance station. **Mouffetard escape**: Street lantern rope cut; Javert misled toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; market-gardens, timber-yards, unpaved roads. **Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (CONVENT CARRIAGE GATE)**: Ajar gate, courtyard, vine-hung walls, tall trees above wall. **Wall (approximately 18 feet)**: Extends from niche to house 49 Rue Polonceau; shorter fragment along Rue Droit-Mur. **CONVENT OF THE BERNARDINES OF THE PERPETUAL ADORATION**: Gloomy building, heavily shuttered window with sheet zinc, ancient cistern pipes, linden-tree with ivy, grated windows, upper story scuttles resembling prison cells. **INTERIOR GARDEN**: Vast oblong area; alley of large poplars; forest trees in corners; solitary gnarled tree, fruit-trees, vegetable beds, melon patch with glass frames, old well, stone benches, grass and green mould. **PARLOR**: Theatre-box-like narrow space; monstrous lattice of iron bars (squares less than 1.5 inches diagonal) riveted by clenched-fist fastenings; behind lattice: barrier of black shutters reinforced with gingerbread-yellow wooden beams, always closed; behind shutters: nun's voice screened by iron grating and plate with thousand holes; slat opens revealing nun's mouth and chin only, covered with black veil, guimpe, shroud; window on world-side only; quadrangular hole one foot square with interlacing iron bars reinforced by sheet of tin with thousand microscopic holes; aperture like letter-box orifice; tape attached to bell-wire.

## Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration (Comprehensive Details)
**Order Lineage**: Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga obedience; Benedictine order founded 529 by Saint-Benoît; spawned nine orders including Cîteaux (1098), Carthusians, Cluny, Saint-Maur, Vallombrosa, Granmont, Célestins, Camaldules, Humiliés, Olivateurs, Silvestrins. **Dress**: Black clothing with white guimpe mounting to chin; serge robe with large sleeves; large woollen veil; band descending over brow; novices wear all-white; professed nuns wear rosary at side. **Austerity**: Fast all year; abstain from meat; additional fasting in Lent; rise one to three a.m. for breviary and matins; sleep year-round on straw between serge sheets; never light fires; never bathe; scourge every Friday; strict silence except brief recreation; wear drugget chemises September 14 (Exaltation of Holy Cross) to Easter—originally year-round but modified due to summer fevers; resumed chemise causes three-to-four-day fever. **Vows**: Obedience, poverty, chastity, perseverance in seclusion. **Operational Rules**: Never see officiating priest (hidden behind nine-foot serge curtain); drop veils during sermons; speak low; walk with eyes down; only diocesan archbishop permitted entry; absolute passive submission to prioress (canonical subjection—at Christ's voice, at gesture, at first sign, immediately with cheerfulness, perseverance, blind obedience, like file in workman's hand); cannot read or write without express permission. **Reparation Practice**: Each nun in turn performs twelve-hour continuous reparation prayer (either 4 p.m. to 4 a.m. or 4 a.m. to 4 p.m.) on knees on stone before Holy Sacrament, hands clasped, rope around neck; when fatigue unbearable, prostrates flat against earth, arms outstretched as cross. **Possessions Rule**: Never say "my"; call everything "our"; if grow attached to petty object, must surrender it immediately. **Lodging**: Cells open; when meeting, one says "Blessed and adored be the most Holy Sacrament of the altar!" other responds "Forever!". **Hourly Bells**: At each hour three supplementary church bell strokes; all interrupt activity and say in unison formula praising Most Holy Sacrament. **Chanting**: Chant offices to solemn psalmody, pure Gregorian chant, full voice throughout; for office of dead adopt tone so low women's voices can barely descend—effect striking and tragic. **Burial Issue**: Vault beneath grand altar for community burials; Government forbids coffin burial in vault, so nuns leave convent when die. **Friday Observances**: High mass, vespers, all offices as on Sunday; observe little festivals; stations in chapel interminable. **Visitor Communication**: Prioress alone holds communication with strangers; permission to men always refused. **Profession Ceremony**: Novice crowned with white roses, hair brushed and curled; prostrates self; great black veil thrown over her; office for dead sung; nuns separate into two files saying "Our sister is dead" and "Our sister is alive in Jesus Christ!". **Pupils**: Conform to all practices except austerities; some former pupils never break habit of saying "forever!" when door knocked; mothers not permitted to embrace them; many wept seeking embrace permissions. **School Details (Écouen model)**: Distinctions made between virgins and florists in processions of Holy Sacrament; "dais" and "censors" held cords and carried incense; pupils sometimes picked forbidden fruit (green apples, spoiled apricots, inhabited pears) from garden alley with shabby fruit-trees, hiding them under pillows to eat in bed or in closets, considered greatest luxuries; young girls addressed daily question "Who is a virgin?". **Archbishop's Visit Observation**: During pastoral visit, pretty little rosy girl with beautiful golden hair entered class-room. **Mademoiselle Bouchard Incident**: Connected with Montmorency family; wagered she would request day's leave of absence (enormity in austere community); when Archbishop M. de Quélen passed pupils, she stepped out of ranks and asked; he smiled, granted three days; prioress could do nothing; caused horror of convent but joy of pupil. **School Mysticism**: Pupils taught prayer "Little white Paternoster, which God made" containing elaborate imagery of angels, Virgin Mary, apostles, virgins, shirts of God's birth, Saint Margaret's cross, encounters with Saint John, promise of paradise.

## Mysterious Resident: Madame Albertine
**Identity and Status**: Woman not a nun, treated with great respect; addressed as Madame Albertine; mysterious mysterious person; hardly thirty years of age; dark complexion; tolerably pretty; contained "arrangements of fortune necessary for a great marriage." **Claimed Condition**: Passed for dead in the world; said to be mad. **Appearance and Behavior**: Vague look in large black eyes; could she see—doubt about this; glided rather than walked; never spoke; not quite known whether she breathed; nostrils livid and pinched as after yielding up last sigh; possessed strange spectral grace; wherever she entered, people felt cold; to touch her hand like touching snow. **Convent Reaction**: Sister on seeing her pass said to another, "She passes for a dead woman"; other replied, "Perhaps she is one." **Social Connection**: One day uttered words "Ah! Auguste!" setting every one in convent who had privilege of speech to chattering; revelations contained in those words; M. de Rohan's name really was Auguste; evident Madame Albertine belonged to very highest society, knew M. de Rohan, spoke familiarly of so great a lord, suggesting close connection—possibly relationship.

## Clerical Visitor: M. de Rohan
**Identity and Status**: Vicar-general of Archbishop of Paris, awaiting episcopate; unknown to himself, object of attention to school-girls. **Habit**: Came tolerably often to celebrate offices in chapel of nuns of Petit-Picpus. **Appearance**: Had sweet and rather shrill voice which young recluses came to know and distinguish; former mousquetaire; said to be very coquettish; handsome brown hair well dressed in roll around head; broad girdle of magnificent moire; black cassock of most elegant cut in world. **Effect on Pupils**: Held great place in imaginations of sixteen-year-old girls; could not see him because of serge curtain. **Connection**: Madame Albertine intimately familiar with him (called him by pet name "Auguste").

## Jean Valjean's Current Sanctuary Status
**ESCAPE FROM M. SUR M.** (January 1823 evening): Successfully fled jail after Javert's arrest beside Fantine's death-bed; climbed 18-foot wall using muscular force; placed Cosette on back; descended safely to interior garden via roof. **REFUGE DISCOVERY AND FAUCHELEVENT**: Encountered elderly crippled gardener Fauchelevent, admitted to convent approximately two years previously (1821) on Mayor Madeleine's recommendation after falling from cart. **PSYCHOLOGICAL STATE**: So long as Cosette near, needs nothing except her, fears nothing except her; experiencing continual tremor. **COSETTE**: Now sleeping in Fauchelevent's bed; rosy; completely dependent on Valjean. **CURRENT LOCATION** (Autumn Year 2): Still secured in convent sanctuary. **ALTERED APPEARANCE**: Sadness, uneasiness, anxiety, depression have altered his walk and impressed senility on bearing.

## Fauchelevent (Elderly Gardener—Established Ally)
**Identity**: Old crippled gardener; admitted to convent approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; calls Valjean "Father Madeleine"; speaks freely about work. **Current Occupation**: Spreading straw mats over melon beds in garden; wears bell and kneecap device. **Hospitality**: Provided Cosette safe bed; offered cheese, black bread, wine. **Status**: Valjean's only known ally and protector in Paris; sole person aware of Valjean and Cosette's presence.

## Javert's Pursuit and Strategic Hesitation
**REASSIGNMENT TO PARIS** (January 1823): When Valjean escaped M. sur M. jail, Javert summoned; attached to Paris police force. **NEWSPAPER REPORT** (December 1823): Newspaper announced Valjean's death; Javert read, remarked "That's a good entry," thought no more. **REACTIVATION**: Police report concerning child abduction in Montfermeil revived Javert's memory; suspected Valjean had sought daughter. **JAVERT'S SECRET INVESTIGATION**: Without telling anyone, took coach to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; got old woman portress talking—she confirmed coat-lined-with-millions episode; hired room, listened at lodger's door; Valjean saw candle through key-hole, foiled spy by silence. **REASONS FOR SECRECY** (Three Motives): (1) Slightest indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) Recapturing ex-convict reputed dead was magnificent success—feared being deprived; (3) Javert, being artist, had taste for unforeseen—hated well-heralded successes, preferred elaborating masterpieces in dark, unveiling suddenly. **PURSUIT ESCALATION**: Following day Valjean noticed five-franc piece falling; old woman suspected lodger intending to leave, warned Javert; at night Javert waited behind trees with two men. **ESCAPE FROM MOUFFETARD**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder in lantern, led astray toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot. **JAVERT'S HESITATION AND PSYCHOLOGICAL TORMENT**: Followed Valjean from tree to tree, had not lost sight single instant; why had not arrested? Still in doubt. **STRATEGIC CALCULATION**: Considered abrupt demand for papers risky—if not Valjean, possibly chief of dangerous band; to arrest hastily would "kill the hen that laid golden eggs." Began the game—experienced ecstatic and infernal moment; allowed man to go ahead, knowing had him safe, gloating with voluptuousness of spider allowing fly to flutter, of cat letting mouse run; claws and talons possess monstrous sensuality. **MOMENT OF LOSS**: Even when saw Valjean escaped, Javert did not lose head; sure convict could not be far off, established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades. **IMPEDIMENT TO ARREST**: Free press embarrassed police; arbitrary arrests denounced by newspapers; interference with individual liberty grave matter; police agents afraid of mistakes; mistake meant dismissal.

## English Harbor Towns Communities (Secondary Setting)
Named residents: Matho Stenson (moved to Yarlby, did not return), Ismira Stenson, Pelde Stenson, Harine Lindmere, Davus Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Yera, Orrald the Younger, Orrald Stenson, Fewyn Stenworth. **Observations and Activities**: Reading almanacs aloud with mispronounced saints (Pelde); sorting letters by candlelight; discussing weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices (Davus and Yera—"price of salt is scandal"); Harine and Orrald noted river up in spring; aching back complaints (Pelde); baker's boy late, line at oven long; rain threatening since morning but holding off; bees humming in lavender; frost silvered hedges; wind from water with salt and tar smell; Pelde hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; children chased hoop down lane shrieking; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; Orrald bought ribbon at stall, regretted it; Harine argued with carter over sack of oats price; Pelde walked long way round to avoid muddy square; Pelde watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly.
